newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's first $100 mln corporate bond covered.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's first $100 mln corporate bond covered.

text.p: Jordan's first corporate bond issue, a $100 million eurobond, was fully subscribed but the country's relatively low credit-risk rating deterred wide global investor interest, bankers and managers said on Friday.
Co-lead managers HSBC Markets and Jordan's Arab Bank jointly launched the five-year floating rate issue (FRN) by Jordan Phosphate Mines on Wednesday.

"The deal was fully sold out on day one...Jordan is totally new for a lot of other investors (besides Middle East) and it was fully subscribed," said Chris O'Malley, Middle East, India, and Africa director at HSBC Markets Limited.

Jordan secured at around 1.5 percent or 150 basis points above LIBOR (London Inter-Bank Offered Rate) a more price competitive spread for the issue than Eastern Europe or Lebanon debt paper, usually above 2 percent.
But Jordan's BB minus credit rating -- below investment grade -- still deterred investors such as U.K. banks to buy the paper because they would have had to take provisions.

"The fact of the matter is that while Jordan has had a superb story in an economic transformation, it's not out of the woods yet. This is still a provisionable security on a long-term asset on the banks books in the U.K.," O'Malley told Reuters.
"At the end of the day it's a double B minus situation still and there are clearly problems, Jordan has a considerable debt burden, one of the highest on a per-capita basis," he added.

But some local bankers also say the tight spread which allowed HSBC to gain the mandate was too low in the first place to attract a wider global base from investors unfamiliar with Jordan. It may also have harmed Jordan's prospects to raise investor appetite for future corporate issues, they said.

"It's good for Jordan but the tight spread may have caused the deal to be distributed mainly to the foreign currency liquid Jordanian banks and a few other investors, " said Khaled Masri, investment manager at Arab-Jordan Investment Bank (AJIB).

Some bankers say as a result the bond issue now appears more of a syndicated loan than a securities issue, adding that HSBC along with local investors had mainly attracted Middle Eastern financial institutions in a few purchases by global banks.
"In terms of the geographic spread, very roughly about 50-60 percent was Middle Eastern related entities, clearly the name was best understood by regional investors," O'Malley said.

HSBC's own allotments were 20 percent distributed in the U.K. and Europe respectively. But HSBC says a significant part was placed in Jordan not of its own choice but because the issuer and the government wanted to involve local banks.
These banks have played a significant role in the issue after Jordan's leading Arab Bank formed a syndicate with them to underwrite as a much as 50 percent of its value. O'Malley said.
HSBC said that the "very well priced deal" was a realistic gauge of demand for Jordanian paper.

HSBC does not expect the issue to hold back a successful launch of Jordan's first $70 million sovereign bond issue by year-end although it could be difficult for the country to get the same pricing as on its first corporate bond issue.
"It's a major step forward for Jordan..I think no one will now doubt Jordan cannot issue in its own right a sovereign paper..I think they can," O'Malley said.
